Content:
Suppose that

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf T: (u,v) \to \left(x(u,v),y(u,v)\right)]

Content:
is a [MATH: C^1] transformation that has no critical points (i.e., it is invertible) inside some region [MATH: \Delta\subset \mathbb R^2,] and that [MATH: \mathbf T(\Delta) = D,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e711b33357673b0c02a3d83ee021cb8b]

Content:
We've already seen how the area of a non-trivial region [MATH: D] can be computed using the change of variables formula:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
We can extend this formula to compute the integral of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] over [MATH: D,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
Note the similarity with the change of variables formula for the integral of a single-variable function [MATH: f(x)] over [MATH: D = (a,b){:}]

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_D f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} f(x(u))\,\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u]

Content:
Applying the change of variables formula is similar to when we were restricting our attention to areas in the plane. The only difference now is that we must also express the integrand [MATH: f(x,y)] in terms of [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]

Consider the region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane, given by
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq 4x+2y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y-x \leq 3 \big\}.]
By performing the change of variables [MATH: u = 4x+2y] and [MATH: v=y - x,] write the following integral in terms of [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]
[MATH: \displaystyle
\iint\limits_D \sin \left(3(x+y)\right) \: \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's define a transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] as follows:

[MATH: [u; v]]

This transformation maps some region [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane to our region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v]

where [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}] is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf{T}.]

Note that the change of variables [MATH: u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x]

gives us the inverse function [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1},] that is

[MATH: [x; y]]

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

Step 1: Find [MATH: \Delta,] which is the image of [MATH: D] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}.]

Our domain in the [MATH: uv]-plane is

[MATH: Δ|= {(u, v): − 2 ≤ u ≤ 2, 0 ≤ v ≤ 3}.]

Step 2: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1}.]

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1}] is [MATH: (∂(u, v))/(∂(x, y))|=|(∂u)/(∂x)|(∂u)/(∂y); (∂v)/(∂x)|(∂v)/(∂y)|; =|4|2; − 1|1|; = 6.]

Step 3: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

Step 4: Perform the change of variables.

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations [MATH: u = 4x+2y, \qquad v = y-x] for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y], which gives [MATH: x = \dfrac{u-2v}6, \qquad y =\dfrac{u+4v}6.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf T: (u,v) \to \left(x(u,v),y(u,v)\right)]

Content:
is a [MATH: C^1] transformation that has no critical points (i.e., it is invertible) inside some region [MATH: \Delta\subset \mathbb R^2,] and that [MATH: \mathbf T(\Delta) = D,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e711b33357673b0c02a3d83ee021cb8b]

Content:
We've already seen how the area of a non-trivial region [MATH: D] can be computed using the change of variables formula:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
We can extend this formula to compute the integral of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] over [MATH: D,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
Note the similarity with the change of variables formula for the integral of a single-variable function [MATH: f(x)] over [MATH: D = (a,b){:}]

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_D f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} f(x(u))\,\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u]

Content:
Applying the change of variables formula is similar to when we were restricting our attention to areas in the plane. The only difference now is that we must also express the integrand [MATH: f(x,y)] in terms of [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]

Content:

[MATH: [u; v]]

This transformation maps some region [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane to our region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v]

where [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}] is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf{T}.]

Note that the change of variables
[MATH: u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x]

[MATH: [x; y]]

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

Step 1: Find [MATH: \Delta,] which is the image of [MATH: D] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}.]

Our domain in the [MATH: uv]-plane is

Step 2: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1}.]

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1}] is

Step 3: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T] is
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{6}.]
Note that [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0] everywhere inside [MATH: \Delta.] In other words, [MATH: \mathbf T] has no critical points inside [MATH: \Delta.]
